sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A distributed transaction is a unit of work that spans multiple independent resources or services (databases, message queues, microservices) yet must preserve ACID-like guarantees; the four canonical approaches are **2PC**, **3PC**, **Saga**, and **TCC (Try-Confirm-Cancel)**, each making a different trade-off between consistency strength, availability, latency, and complexity.

A distributed transaction is the moment a single business operation stops fitting inside one database. When a customer places an Amazon order, the system must deduct inventory in the warehouse service, reserve payment in the billing service, schedule shipment in the logistics service, and write an audit row in the finance ledger — each living in its own database. If any one fails, the partial work must be undone; otherwise you get paid without shipping, or ship without being paid. The traditional ACID recipe — locks, write-ahead logs, and crash recovery — works beautifully inside one process because the database owns all the locks and can abort by rolling back its own log. Once the operation spans processes, those guarantees fall apart: there is no global lock manager, no shared write-ahead log, no global clock, and the network can drop messages between any two participants at any moment. The architect's job is to choose a protocol that approximates ACID across these boundaries without sacrificing the system's availability or latency budget.

The fundamental challenge is atomicity across failure boundaries. If the payment service commits but the shipping service is down, you cannot "leave the transaction half-committed" — you must either complete it later (eventual consistency) or undo it (compensation). The CAP theorem compounds the problem: during a network partition, you cannot have both availability and consistency, so any distributed transaction protocol must pick one. The classical database world picked consistency, producing Two-Phase Commit (2PC): a coordinator asks all participants to "prepare" (promise to commit), and only when every participant has prepared does the coordinator say "commit." 2PC gives strong atomicity, but it is a blocking protocol — if the coordinator crashes after participants have prepared, they hold their locks indefinitely, waiting for the coordinator to recover. This is the "blocking on coordinator failure" problem that makes 2PC ill-suited for high-availability microservices. Three-Phase Commit (3PC) attempts to fix this with a third "pre-commit" phase and timeouts, so participants can recover without the coordinator — but 3PC still fails under network partitions (the very scenario it claims to handle), so it is rarely used in practice.

The microservices world picked availability, producing the Saga pattern. A saga breaks the global transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each committed independently. If a later step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions to semantically undo the earlier ones — e.g., if shipping fails, the saga issues a refund. Sagas trade ACID atomicity for eventual consistency: there is a window where intermediate state is visible, and compensation is not a true rollback (you cannot unsend an email). This is acceptable for most business workflows because the alternative — holding locks across services for the duration of a multi-second operation — is operationally untenable. Sagas come in two flavors: choreography (each service emits an event triggering the next) and orchestration (a central orchestrator calls each service and tracks state). Orchestration is generally preferred for complex flows because it makes the workflow explicit, debuggable, and easier to evolve.

TCC (Try-Confirm-Cancel) is a fourth approach that splits each step into two phases: a Try phase that reserves resources (e.g., hold $100 on a credit card) and a Confirm or Cancel phase that finalizes or releases. TCC gives stronger isolation than saga (resources are reserved, not consumed, until confirm), at the cost of every service implementing three operations instead of one. It is widely used in Chinese fintech (Alipay, WeChat Pay) and is gaining traction in Western microservice frameworks like Seata and DTM. Compared to 2PC, TCC is non-blocking and operationally simpler; compared to saga, it has cleaner semantics for resource reservation but is more code-intensive. The trade-off matrix is roughly: 2PC for strong consistency within a single datacenter (XA transactions in Java EE, PostgreSQL prepared transactions); 3PC in theory but rarely in practice; saga for cross-service workflows that tolerate eventual consistency; TCC for resource-reservation semantics where isolation matters more than simplicity.

The real-world anchor is Amazon's order pipeline. The checkout flow touches at least four systems: payments (charge the card), inventory (decrement stock), shipping (schedule pickup), and notifications (send confirmation email). Amazon uses an event-driven saga: the Order service writes a "OrderCreated" event, which triggers the Payment service to charge, which emits "PaymentSucceeded" or "PaymentFailed," which triggers Inventory to commit or release the hold, and so on. If Payment fails, the saga compensates by releasing the inventory hold and marking the order as failed. The customer sees the order go from "Pending" to "Failed" within seconds, never having to wonder whether the system will silently lose money. The lesson for architects is that distributed transactions are not about choosing the "best" protocol — they are about choosing the protocol whose trade-offs match the business's tolerance for inconsistency, latency, and operational complexity, and being explicit about the consistency guarantees you can and cannot provide.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Client Request
Place Order] --> B{Choose Protocol} B -->|Strong Consistency| C[2PC / 3PC] B -->|Eventual Consistency| D[Saga] B -->|Resource Reservation| E[TCC] C --> C1[Coordinator: PREPARE all] C1 --> C2{All prepared?} C2 -->|Yes| C3[COMMIT all] C2 -->|No| C4[ABORT all] C3 --> Z[Done - ACID] C4 --> Z D --> D1[Step 1: Reserve Inventory] D1 --> D2[Step 2: Charge Payment] D2 -->|Success| D3[Step 3: Schedule Shipping] D2 -->|Fail| D5[Compensate: Release Inventory] D3 --> Z2[Done - Eventual] D5 --> Z3[Done - Rolled back] E --> E1[Try: Hold $100 on card] E1 --> E2{All Try ok?} E2 -->|Yes| E3[Confirm: Capture $100] E2 -->|No| E4[Cancel: Release hold] E3 --> Z4[Done - Reserved then committed] E4 --> Z4 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +---+ +---+ +---+ | I | --> | P | --> | S | I=Inventory, P=Payment, S=Shipping +---+ +---+ +---+ | | | v v v +---+ +---+ +---+ |rsv| |chg| |sch| reserve(), charge(), schedule() +---+ +---+ +---+ | | | if charge() fails: |<---------| compensating flow v +---+ |rel| <-- release() compensates reserve() +---+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The client (e.g., a checkout button) initiates a distributed transaction that must touch Inventory, Payment, and Shipping services — each with its own database. 2. The architect chooses a protocol based on trade-offs: 2PC/3PC for strong ACID, Saga for eventual consistency with compensation, TCC for resource reservation semantics. 3. If Saga is chosen: Inventory reserves stock (local commit), Payment charges the card (local commit), Shipping schedules pickup (local commit). If Payment fails, the saga runs the compensating action "release inventory" to undo step 1 — the system reaches a consistent (rolled-back) state without ever holding cross-service locks.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Distributed transaction approaches: a mock comparison of 2PC, Saga, and TCC.
Each approach handles the same 'place order' flow across 3 services.
"""

class Service:
    """A mock microservice with its own local state."""
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.state = {}          # committed state
        self.reserved = {}       # TCC try-phase reservations

# --- 2PC: blocking, strong consistency ---
def two_phase_commit(services, txid, ops):
    coordinator = "TC"
    print(f"[2PC] {coordinator} -> PREPARE {txid}")
    prepared = []
    for svc, op in zip(services, ops):
        if op(svc, dry_run=True):    # participant promises to commit
            prepared.append(svc)
            print(f"  [{svc.name}] PREPARED")
        else:
            print(f"  [{svc.name}] ABORT (cannot prepare)")
            break
    if len(prepared) == len(services):
        print(f"[2PC] {coordinator} -> COMMIT {txid}")
        for svc, op in zip(services, ops):
            op(svc, dry_run=False)   # participant commits
        return "COMMITTED"
    print(f"[2PC] {coordinator} -> ABORT {txid}")
    return "ABORTED"

# --- Saga: eventual consistency, with compensation ---
def saga(services, ops, compensations):
    done = []
    for svc, op in zip(services, ops):
        if op(svc):                  # local commit
            done.append(svc)
            print(f"  [Saga] {svc.name} step OK")
        else:
            print(f"  [Saga] {svc.name} step FAILED -> compensate")
            for svc_done, comp in zip(reversed(done), reversed(compensations[:len(done)])):
                comp(svc_done)       # semantic undo
                print(f"  [Saga] compensate {svc_done.name}")
            return "ROLLED BACK"
    return "COMMITTED"

# --- TCC: try / confirm / cancel ---
def tcc(services, try_ops, confirm_ops, cancel_ops):
    tried = []
    for svc, t in zip(services, try_ops):
        if t(svc):                   # reserve resources
            tried.append(svc)
        else:
            for svc_tried, c in zip(tried, cancel_ops[:len(tried)]):
                c(svc_tried)         # cancel reservations
            return "CANCELLED"
    for svc, f in zip(services, confirm_ops):
        f(svc)                       # finalize reservations
    return "CONFIRMED"

# --- Demo ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    inv, pay, ship = Service("Inventory"), Service("Payment"), Service("Shipping")
    print("--- 2PC ---")
    two_phase_commit([inv, pay, ship], "TX1",
                     [lambda s, dry_run: True,
                      lambda s, dry_run: False,    # payment fails
                      lambda s, dry_run: True])
    print("\n--- Saga ---")
    saga([inv, pay, ship],
         [lambda s: True, lambda s: False, lambda s: True],
         [lambda s: print(f"     release stock in {s.name}"),
          lambda s: None, lambda s: None])
```

quiz.explanation: 2PC is blocking because a participant that has voted "prepared" in phase 1 must hold its locks and wait for the coordinator's phase-2 decision (commit or abort). If the coordinator crashes after the participant has prepared, the participant cannot unilaterally decide — it does not know whether other participants voted yes or no, and it cannot reach the coordinator.

quiz.explanation: A compensating transaction is a semantic undo — a new transaction that logically reverses the effect of an earlier committed transaction, rather than a physical rollback that erases the earlier transaction's writes. The difference matters because the earlier transaction has already committed and may have been observed by other services or external systems.
